title: Lawrence Marrero's banjo approach and teaching
summary: Lawrence's relaxed, cool attitude, muted banjo, stroking technique, simple method lessons, awareness of his limits and sketchy harmony knowledge.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: What did he teach you in, uh, in the very fundamental technical things I'm talking about? Uh, not just, just start at the beginning, before you ever got into anything like harmony, just, how to hold your banjo and how to stroke it.

Yeah, this was very interesting. He taught me, uh, he didn't teach exactly. I sort of observed. Uh, he had a very relaxed, uh, I don't give a damn attitude towards, towards playing. No, that's, that's not the right word. Uh, you know, it's not that he didn't give a damn. He, he, he just, he just kind of, he just kind of realized that, that swinging was a very natural thing. And no amount of foot stomping and, and, uh, uh, exaggerated, uh, exaggerated activity was going to make you swing. It was a very natural thing. And I sort of observed this in him. And this got to me. And I think, I think he had the, what has been called in bop musicians, the cool attitude. I think Emile Barnes had it. The cool attitude. Uh, it's just the, a very natural thing.

Well, they were restrained and casual to me. Yeah. Look at guys like that. Yeah. I mean they weren't trying to prove anything to anybody. Right. Exactly. That's what it meant. They felt like stomping their foot, they would.

If they didn't, they wouldn't. Right. That's just what it meant. That is the cool attitude, as far as I'm concerned. Well, uh, how did you hold your banjo? Oh, just the ordinary way. On the, uh, on the right thigh. It usually crossed my leg and just the way I hold a guitar, usually put it on the right thigh. And, uh, Lawrence used to use, uh, a mute on his banjo, which sort of put it halfway between, and this is in, uh, relation to timbre, put it halfway between guitar and banjo. It had more of a legato feeling than a, uh, in this, this choppy banjo feeling, which was very rhythmic, you know? And, and the tones were sustained. And it was a very, a very pretty sound, in that sense. A very, a very, uh, smooth sound. But very rhythmic, too.
Did he hit it up towards the neck, or hit it down low, or where he was stroking?

He used to hit it sort of about in the middle of the, between the bridge and where the neck would begin. Somewhere between there, where it's about the right place to hit it, to stroke it. And they didn't use any particular kind of pick or anything. And, uh, he was playing this very simple, basically because he didn't have the technique and he knew it. Uh, but he, he just had this, this very natural, this very natural thing going, very casual thing going. And so, actually, the, the teaching amounted to, to just going through this banjo method. And then after we'd go through a few little tunes, you know, and just play blues, uh, play, uh, I, uh, I improvise on different, uh, traditional things. Then I'd sit in with Lewis's band, and that sort of thing.
I noticed he, uh, one day he'd tell me, he said he wished he could solo more than he did, but he, he, uh, just said that he never was much of a solo.
No, he realized his limitations, you know. And, uh, he made no bones about it, you know. He, uh, he, uh, just knew where he stood and he knew where others stood.
Well, how was his knowledge of harmony?

That's kind of vague to me. I don't remember. I think he had a, a kind of a sketchy knowledge, uh, theoretical knowledge. He, uh, he knew about the, uh, relative family of chords and, uh, and just, uh, just the, just the very basic knowledge, what he needed to get by, I think. Uh, it wasn't, uh, it wasn't a very, a very, a very grounded knowledge or a very formal knowledge. But he did have a knowledge of, of chordal relationships, definitely.
